issues.description: ACL.root field complects authorization decision, namespace identity, and a 'this is a root policy' flag in one nullable pointer
issues.detail: The `root` field was a clean boolean predicate ('does this ACL grant root?'). It now carries three concerns at once: (1) is this a root policy? (2) which namespace owns the root? (3) implicit ancestry-based authorization scope. A nil/non-nil *namespace.Namespace is being used as both a boolean and a value carrier. That's a textbook complecting: presence-of-policy is now intertwined with namespace identity, and readers must know the convention 'nil means not-root, non-nil means root scoped to this ns'. Decompose into two fields — `isRoot bool` and `rootNamespace *namespace.Namespace` — or better, an explicit small struct `rootScope { ns *Namespace }` where presence is the predicate and the field name says what it is. The nil-pointer-as-boolean idiom is easy (familiar Go) but not simple.

issues.description: NamespaceSealed is a stub that silently lies — returns false unconditionally with a TODO, while callers will treat its answer as fact
issues.detail: `func (c *Core) NamespaceSealed(ns *namespace.Namespace) bool { return false }` is place-oriented programming at its worst: a function that pretends to compute a fact about the world but returns a constant. ListAllNamespaces is described as 'including sealed namespaces (currently stubbed with NamespaceSealed stub)' — meaning downstream code is being wired against a method whose semantics will change later. This is the opposite of thinking first. Either (a) don't add the call sites yet, (b) return an error 'not implemented' so callers fail loud, or (c) make it `func NamespaceSealed(...) (bool, error)` so the eventual real implementation can report storage failures without a breaking signature change. As written, when SealManager lands, every caller becomes a silent behavior change.

issues.description: Authorization fast-path now depends on namespace ancestry computed inside AllowOperation; the time-of-check vs time-of-use semantics are unclear
issues.detail: The root fast-path previously was a single boolean read. It now computes `ns.HasParent(a.root)` on every request, where both `ns` (from request context) and `a.root` (captured at policy load time) are *namespace.Namespace pointers. Two questions Hickey would ask before merging: (1) Is `a.root` a value or an identity? If the namespace it points to is renamed/moved/deleted between ACL construction and AllowOperation, what's the correct answer? (2) Is HasParent reflexive — does a namespace 'have itself' as parent? The test only covers ns1 (a direct child of root context); it does not cover ns==a.root nor deeply nested grandchild paths. Make the value semantics explicit: capture `rootNamespaceID string` and `rootNamespacePath string` at construction, compare by ID/path prefix at check time. Don't carry a pointer to a mutable identity into an authorization decision.

issues.description: Removed invariant 'root policy only allowed in root namespace' without a replacement check on who can create one
issues.detail: Previously NewACL rejected a root policy outside the root namespace. That check is now gone — any namespace context can construct an ACL with a root policy and it will be honored within that namespace subtree. The PR says this 'enables namespace-owned root token generation' but the guard that ensured only authorized callers could mint such an ACL has been removed without a stated replacement. Where does the authorization to attach a root policy now live? If the answer is 'in the not-yet-implemented SealManager / token generator', then this PR ships the capability before the gate. State the invariant explicitly in code (a comment naming where the upstream check must live) or keep the guard until the upstream check exists.

issues.description: Switch-case rewrite of AdjustErrorStatusCode quietly changes precedence semantics from 'apply all matching' to 'first match wins'
issues.detail: The previous code was a sequence of independent `if errwrap.Contains(...)` blocks — each could fire, and the HTTPCoded passthrough at the end could override earlier status assignments. The new `switch { case ...: case ...: }` short-circuits: only the first matching case runs. If an error both wraps ErrSealed AND implements HTTPCodedError, the old code would let HTTPCoded win; the new code locks in 503 and never reaches the HTTPCoded branch. That is a behavior change disguised as a refactor. Either preserve the original semantics (keep them as independent ifs) or document and test the new precedence order explicitly.

issues.description: NSTokenLength = TokenLen + "."[1] + nsID encodes structure into a length constant; the token format is now implicit and place-oriented
issues.detail: The description introduces `NSTokenLength` as `(TokenLen + "."[1] + nsID)`. This is treating the dot separator as a length contribution and the namespace ID as having a fixed length — both are structural facts about token encoding being smuggled into an arithmetic expression. What is the value here? A token. What is its structure? `<token>.<nsID>`. Then the right primitives are an encode function and a decode function returning (token, nsID, error), with the length derivable from those, not the other way around. Defining the constant first invites every reader to depend on the wrong invariant. Hammock this: write the codec, not the length.

issues.description: Wholesale s/namespaceMountEntryView/NamespaceView(barrier, ns).SubView(...)/ pushes barrier choice to call sites
issues.detail: Removing `namespaceMountEntryView` and inlining `NamespaceView(c.barrier, ns).SubView(prefix)` at every call site means each caller must now know (a) which barrier to use and (b) the full prefix string. The previous method encapsulated both. Two readings: the new form is more transparent (good — values flowing through), or it's more brittle (every new call site can pick the wrong barrier or mistype the prefix). Pick a side: if transparency is the goal, define small named view constructors like `passwordPolicyView(core, ns)` so the prefix string isn't repeated. Otherwise expect drift.

issues.description: Mechanical context.Background() -> namespace.RootContext(...) test churn signals that namespace is now an ambient requirement; consider making it explicit in signatures
issues.detail: Dozens of test sites are being rewritten from `context.Background()` to `namespace.RootContext(...)` because functions now require a namespace in context. That's a value (the namespace) being passed through an identity channel (the context). Easy (Go convention) but not simple. Each function that requires a namespace could take `ns *Namespace` as an explicit parameter — then no context plumbing, no 'forgot to wrap' bugs, no test churn on every signature reach. The current direction doubles down on context-as-grab-bag. Worth a hammock before the pattern calcifies across the codebase.

review.summary: This PR is doing real work — separating the root-policy concept from the root namespace is the right direction. But it ships several COMPLECTED and PLACE-ORIENTED constructs that will be painful to undo. The most serious: `ACL.root` now uses a nullable *Namespace pointer as both a boolean predicate and an identity carrier (decompose into explicit fields), and `Core.NamespaceSealed` is a stub returning a constant that downstream code already calls as if it were a fact — that's INCIDENTAL-COMPLEXITY masquerading as a feature flag. The response_util.go refactor from independent ifs to a switch silently changes precedence and is EASY-NOT-SIMPLE. The dropped invariant 'root policy only allowed in root namespace' needs a stated replacement gate, not a TODO. The question that should have been asked first: what are the *values* here — what is a token, what is a namespace, what is 'sealed', what is 'root' — and which of them are identities (mutable references) vs values (immutable facts)? Until those are named, every test-churn commit and every stub method is paying interest on a debt that hasn't been counted.
